cau.chu: Napoleon marched into Russia with over 600,000 men, and six months later fewer than 10,000 could still fight.
su_that: Napoleon's initial force upon entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men

cau.chu: By 1812 Napoleon owned most of Europe, and Russia was the holdout.
su_that: orchestrated numerous military campaigns that led to the establishment of the First French Empire

cau.chu: Russia had quit his blockade of Britain, which Napoleon took personally.
su_that: Tsar Alexander to break away from the Continental blockade on 31 December 1810

cau.chu: So he gathered the largest army the continent had ever seen, from a dozen nations.
su_that: over 150,000 horses, approximately 25,000 wagons, and nearly 1,400 artillery pieces

cau.chu: The plan was simple: crush the Russians in one battle, dictate terms, and go home.
su_that: to defeat the Imperial Russian Army and compel Tsar Alexander I to rejoin to the Continental System

cau.chu: On 24 June 1812, the first columns crossed the Neman, and the bad idea began.
su_that: Beginning on 24 June 1812, the initial wave of the multinational Grande Armée crossed the Neman River

cau.chu: Facing him were two Russian armies that had no intention of fighting on his schedule.
su_that: Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration totaling approximately 180,000–220,000 soldiers

cau.chu: Instead he got a burning Moscow and a peace offer that never came.
su_that: Remaining in Moscow for five weeks, Napoleon awaited a peace proposal that never materialized

cau.chu: Then came the snow, the hunger, and the Cossacks, none of which appeared in the plan.
su_that: combined with guerilla warfare from Russian peasants and Cossacks, resulted in significant losses

cau.chu: More than half of the soldiers perished from starvation, exhaustion, typhus and the climate.
su_that: More than half of the soldiers perished from starvation, exhaustion, typhus, and the unforgiving continental climate

cau.chu: On 5 December, Napoleon left his army at Smorgonie in a sled, bound for Paris.
su_that: On 5 December, Napoleon departed from the army at Smorgonie in a sled and returned to Paris

cau.chu: By December the survivors staggered back across the frozen Neman, and the army was gone.
su_that: The remnants of the principal armies, disheartened, crossed the frozen Neman and the Bug

cau.chu: He wanted one decisive battle, but the decisive thing turned out to be winter.
This is how the greatest military mind of his generation walked into the greatest catastrophe of his career.
su_that: This catastrophic outcome shattered Napoleon's once-untarnished reputation of invincibility

cau.chu: On June 24th, 1812, Napoleon crossed the Neman River with the largest army Europe had ever seen.
su_that: On Wednesday, 24 June [O.S. 12 June] 1812 with Napoleon's army crossing the border

cau.chu: Half a million men, 150,000 horses, 25,000 wagons, all flooding into Russia at once.

The lack of horses to transport food supplies meant that he was forced to abandon up to 100 guns and up to 500 artillery wagons

cau.chu: Napoleon expected a fight at the border, a glorious clash to end the war in weeks.

cau.chu: Instead, the Russians turned around and ran.

cau.chu: Bagration retreated south, refusing every chance to engage despite orders to attack.

This stream of confused orders to Bagration had him upset with Barclay

cau.chu: The French kept marching deeper into Russia, chasing an enemy that would not stop running.

Napoleon pressed his army on after the Russians

su_that: The corps of Barclay and Bagration finally succeeded in uniting in Smolensk

su_that: In the morning of the 16th, Murat's cavalry and Ney's infantry closed up to the western side of Smolensk

The Battle of Smolensk (1812) on August 16–18 became the first real confrontation of significant forces

cau.chu: Napoleon began the attack on the Smolensk Kremlin, and two days of brutal fighting followed.
su_that: Napoleon began the attack on the Smolensk Kremlin

cau.chu: In the middle of the night, Barclay withdrew his troops from the burning city to avoid encirclement.
su_that: In the middle of the night, Barclay de Tolly withdrew his troops from the burning city to avoid a large confrontation with no chance of victory

cau.chu: The Russians slipped away again.
su_that: When the French army moved in, the Russians left to the east

cau.chu: Smolensk was supposed to be the supply hub that would save the campaign and serve as winter quarters.
su_that: According to Antoine-Henri Jomini, Napoleon planned not to go further than Smolensk and make Vilnius his headquarters for the winter

cau.chu: Instead, it was burning rubble.
Napoleon stood at a crossroads: stop here and dig in for winter, or keep chasing the Russians toward Moscow.
Murat implored him to stop, but Napoleon was intent on reaching Moscow.
su_that: Murat implored him to stop, but Napoleon was intent on reaching Moscow

cau.chu: Moscow was only 250 miles away.
On August 24, the Grande Armée marched out on the Old Smolensk Road, heading east toward the capital.
su_that: On 24 August, the Grande Armée marched out on the Old Smolensk Road

cau.chu: On September 7, seventy miles west of Moscow, the Russians finally stopped running.
su_that: Borodino represented the last Russian effort at stopping the French advance on Moscow

cau.chu: Kutuzov, the new commander, spent days piling up earthworks, since the Tsar would not accept another retreat.
su_that: Starting on 3 September, Kutuzov strengthened the line with earthworks

cau.chu: Some 120,000 Russians stood against 130,000 French, and neither side had come to discuss terms.
su_that: by which time the ratio of French to Russian forces had shrunk from 3:1 to 5:4

cau.chu: Fourteen hours of slaughter followed.
su_that: The battle began at 06:00 with the opening of the 102-gun French grand battery

cau.chu: Artillery tore apart infantry in the open, and the field offered very little else to stand behind.
su_that: the Borodino field was too open and had too few natural obstacles

cau.chu: Cavalry charged into walls of musket fire, and the heaps of bodies made every next charge harder.
su_that: Infantry and cavalry had difficulty maneuvering over the heaps of corpses and masses of wounded

cau.chu: The flèches changed hands again and again, with Bagration counterattacking and Ney taking them right back.
su_that: Prince Bagration quickly led a counterattack that threw the French out of the positions

cau.chu: The fight rolled from the flèches on the left to the Raevsky redoubt in the center.
su_that: The Russian center was defended by the Raevsky Redoubt, a massive open-backed earthwork

cau.chu: By dusk, more than 70,000 men lay dead or wounded, and dozens of them were generals.
su_that: this was the bloodiest battle of this series of conflicts with combined casualties between 72,000 and 73,000

cau.chu: Napoleon won the field, but when Ney begged him to send in the Imperial Guard, he said no.
su_that: Napoleon rejected another such request, this time from Marshal Ney.

cau.chu: His excuse was that he did not want the Guard blown up, so far from France.
su_that: I will most definitely not; I do not want to have it blown up.

cau.chu: The Russian army limped away the next day, battered but alive, and took the road east toward Moscow.
su_that: On September 8, the Russian army moved away from the battlefield in twin columns

cau.chu: Kutuzov knew exactly what he was doing: fight once, retreat with the army intact, and let Napoleon stretch his supply lines.
su_that: by fighting the pitched battle, he could now retreat with the Russian army still intact

cau.chu: That decision would haunt him.
su_that: widely criticized by historians as a large blunder

cau.chu: On September 14, Napoleon rode into Moscow expecting a delegation, or at least some applause.
su_that: he was surprised to have received no delegation from the city

cau.chu: Moscow had held roughly 270,000 people, and nearly every one of them was gone.
su_that: the city had a population of approximately 270,000 people

cau.chu: That night, fires started, and by morning Moscow was an inferno with a helpful wind.
su_that: More wind and massive fires.

cau.chu: Rostopchin, the governor, had ordered it, which is one way to say goodbye to home.
su_that: orders had been given by the Governor of the city and the police that the whole city should be burnt

cau.chu: Warehouses, homes, even the fire pumps were wrecked or torched, just to be thorough.
su_that: their equipment had previously either been removed or destroyed on Rostopchin's orders

cau.chu: Napoleon watched from the Kremlin, horrified that anyone would burn their own city and palaces.
su_that: And they did this themselves! So many palaces!

cau.chu: When the fires died, three-quarters of Moscow was ash, and the victory parade was cancelled.
su_that: three quarters of Moscow was reduced to ashes by arson
